strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: enabling reliable self-verification in small language models without relying on larger judge/verifier models, which has clear practical value for efficient deployment.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three model families (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) and three benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), with both PRM and GenRM verifier types, showing consistent improvements from tool integration.
The headline result that a 1B model with ToolV can match or exceed an 8B model under test-time scaling is a compelling and practically significant demonstration of the method's value.

Thorough set of ablations and analyses: performance breakdown by MATH problem category/difficulty, effect of verifier model size scaling, data efficiency of distillation, confusion matrices for verifier accuracy, and qualitative success/failure case studies with concrete transcripts.
Reasonably clear method formulation with a two-stage filtering + scoring pipeline, and good engineering details (multi-LoRA distillation, prompts, hyperparameters) supporting reproducibility.
Extends tool-integration ideas (previously used mainly for generation) specifically to the verification/self-checking side, which is a distinct and useful framing.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Section 5) is built on a highly simplified toy task (verifying a+b=c) and a generic best-of-N monotonicity result borrowed from prior work (Beirami et al.); the connection between these idealized results and the paper's actual complex verification tasks (multi-step math reasoning, fact-checking) is asserted rather than rigorously established, making the theory feel more illustrative than load-bearing.

The tool-based verifier largely re-derives an independent solution via generated code rather than directly checking the specific reasoning steps in the given candidate solution y; this is conceptually closer to a consistency check against an independently computed answer than a faithful verification of the model's stated reasoning, which is a subtle but important limitation not fully discussed.

MMLU-Pro results (Figure 6/12) are noisy and the gains from retrieved-document ToolV are inconsistent across domains (e.g., minimal or negligible improvement in some settings), weakening the generalization claim to knowledge-intensive tasks beyond math.

Gains are markedly smaller on the easier GSM8K benchmark and even degrade at the hardest MATH difficulty level (Level 5), suggesting the method's benefit is concentrated in a specific mid-difficulty regime rather than broadly robust.

No strong baseline comparison against tool-integrated generation approaches (e.g., PAL/ToRA-style code-augmented generators) is provided; it is unclear how much of the benefit could instead be obtained by giving the generator (not just the verifier) tool access, which would be an important ablation/baseline.

Distillation relies on a single, relatively modest teacher (gpt-4o-mini) for verification signals and code generation; the quality ceiling imposed by this teacher is not analyzed with stronger teachers, and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported to assess statistical robustness.

The filtering-only design cannot recover false negatives (correct solutions wrongly rejected by ToolV), which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but do not empirically quantify how often this occurs or its impact on overall Best-of-N ceiling performance.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: enabling small language models to self-verify solutions during test-time scaling without relying on large external verifiers, which matters for efficient/on-device deployment.

Fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation across three base models (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B), two verifier types (PRM, GenRM), and three benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), with consistent improvements from adding the tool-based filter.

Includes useful auxiliary analyses: performance breakdown by problem category/difficulty, effect of verifier scale, data efficiency of distillation, and qualitative success/failure case studies that honestly discuss when the tool-based verifier fails (e.g., incorrect generated code causing false negatives).

The framing of tool use as an 'additional axis' for test-time scaling, together with a (simplified) theoretical account connecting memorization requirements to tool access, provides at least some formal motivation for the empirical design.
weaknesses: The core technical idea—offloading numerical/factual verification to code interpreters or retrievers—is a fairly natural and previously explored idea (PAL, ToRA, Toolformer, tool-augmented reward modeling); the paper's contribution is largely an application/combination of existing techniques (tool-filtering + RM scoring + LoRA-based distillation) rather than a fundamentally new method.

The theoretical analysis (Lemma 5.1/Theorem 5.2 on memorization, Theorem 5.3 on imperfect verifiers) relies on highly simplified toy settings (e.g., verifying a+b=c, binary generator with i.i.d. verifier noise) that only loosely correspond to the actual multi-step, compositional verification tasks used in experiments; the connection between the theory and the empirical system is more illustrative than rigorously predictive.

The headline claim that a 1B model with T1 'outperforms' the 8B model is based on comparing a heavily engineered pipeline (test-time scaling with N up to 64, tool-integrated filtering, and knowledge-distilled verifiers) against the 8B model's single greedy decode; this is not an apples-to-apples comparison and overstates the significance of the result.

The method is described as 'self-verification' but actually depends critically on distillation from a stronger teacher model (GPT-4o-mini and a 7B PRM) to produce usable tool-calling and verification behavior; this conflicts somewhat with the 'self' framing and raises questions about how much of the improvement is attributable to the tool versus the distilled teacher supervision.

ToolV acts only as a binary rejection filter and cannot recover from false negatives, and the reported precision/recall numbers (Table 3) show meaningfully low recall, meaning correct solutions are sometimes discarded—this limitation is acknowledged but not mitigated, and its practical impact on end-task accuracy is not fully quantified.

Generalization to knowledge-intensive tasks (MMLU-Pro) is weak and unstable, with the paper resorting to 'gold documents' (generated by GPT-4o) to show an unrealistic upper bound rather than demonstrating robust improvements under realistic retrieval conditions.

No direct comparison to existing tool-integrated reasoning/verification baselines (e.g., ToRA-style tool-integrated reasoning, tool-augmented reward models) is provided; baselines are limited to majority voting and distilled PRM/GenRM without tools, making it hard to assess how much of the gain is specific to this paper's design versus generic tool integration.

Scale of experimentation is narrow (models only up to 1B for the full T1 pipeline; the 3B/8B comparison in Figure 8 only scales the verifier, not the full system), limiting confidence that findings generalize beyond the specific small-model regime tested.

strengths: Well-motivated research question (self-verification capability of small LMs under test-time scaling) that is timely and underexplored relative to prior work focusing on large verifiers.
Clean two-stage design (ToolV filtering + RM-based scoring) that is simple to implement and integrates with both PRM and GenRM verifiers.

Provides theoretical grounding (memorization bound via mutual information argument, and a toy monotonicity result for imperfect verifiers) that gives some formal intuition for why tool use should help, complementing the empirical results.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across multiple base models (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B), multiple benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), and multiple verifier types (PRM, GenRM), with a striking headline result that a distilled 1B model with ToolV can match/exceed an 8B model.

Good set of supporting analyses: category/difficulty breakdown, verifier-size scaling, distillation data efficiency, confusion matrices, and qualitative case studies (including failure cases) that add credibility and transparency.
Reasonably strong reproducibility support via detailed appendix (prompts, hyperparameters, dataset splits, training setup).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: tool-integrated reasoning/verification (PAL, ToRA, Toolformer, tool-augmented reward modeling) is well established; the core contribution here is largely combining known ingredients (external tool calls + knowledge distillation + best-of-N) specifically for small models, which somewhat limits the conceptual novelty.

The theoretical analysis, while a nice addition, is based on very simplified toy settings (an arithmetic sum-lookup task and a binary generator/imperfect-verifier model) that only loosely correspond to the real verification setting; it mainly formalizes an intuitive claim rather than yielding new non-obvious insight.

ToolV as implemented is a strict rejection filter with no mechanism to recover false negatives, and the paper's own results show performance degradation on harder problems (Level 5) and some categories (Geometry), suggesting the method's benefits are somewhat narrow/task-dependent.
The framework assumes the required external tool is known and well-matched to the verification need a priori, which limits generality to open-ended domains where the appropriate tool is not obvious.

MMLU-Pro experiments are limited (only 3 domains), noisy/unstable per the authors' own admission, and rely on a fairly minimal retrieval pipeline (BM25 without reranking/query transformation); the large gap between retrieved-doc and gold-doc results suggests much of the potential is unrealized in practice.

Distillation depends on a single proprietary teacher (gpt-4o-mini) with no ablation across teacher models, raising questions about sensitivity/generality of the distillation approach and reproducibility with different teachers.

Limited discussion of the added inference-time cost/latency of tool calls (code generation + execution, or retrieval) relative to accuracy gains, especially given the already expensive N=64 best-of-N setup; a cost-normalized comparison would strengthen the practical significance claims.

Since much of the improvement stems from external tool outputs plus teacher-distilled behavior rather than an intrinsic self-verification capability learned by the small model, the framing as "self-verification" is somewhat overstated.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem framing supported by a convincing concept-proof experiment (Figure 1) showing sLMs fail at memorization-heavy verification (arithmetic) while tool-augmented verification closes the gap with larger models.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three model families (Llama-3.2, Qwen2.5, SmolLM2) at multiple scales, two verifier types (PRM and GenRM), and multiple benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, and MMLU-Pro in the appendix), showing consistent gains from the proposed two-stage ToolV framework.

Strong headline results: a 1B model with ToolV matches or outperforms an 8B model, and the paper carefully addresses the natural objection about extra compute overhead via a compute-normalized comparison (Section 6.4, Figure 10/11).

Good breadth of supporting analyses: problem category/difficulty breakdown, verifier-size scaling, filter-effectiveness distribution, data efficiency of distillation, ablation isolating the necessity of the two-stage design, and comparison to a relevant prior tool-integrated verifier baseline (Themis).

Reasonably transparent reproducibility materials — detailed prompts, hyperparameters, and dataset splits are provided in the appendix, and the paper includes qualitative failure-case analysis (Appendix F/G) that adds honesty about the method's limitations.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Section 5) is built on a highly simplified toy setting (verifying a+b=c) and the main theorem (5.2) is close to definitional: if a tool perfectly determines correctness, no memorization is required. This provides limited additional insight beyond the intuition already established empirically, and the connection between the toy proofs and the practical multi-stage pipeline is loose.

Novelty relative to prior tool-integrated verification/reasoning work (PAL, ToRA, CRITIC, Themis) is incremental; the core contribution is largely a two-stage combination of an existing tool-based filter with existing PRM/GenRM verifiers rather than a fundamentally new verification mechanism.

The method depends heavily on distillation from a large proprietary teacher (gpt-4o-mini) for both ToolV and RM-based verifier training, which somewhat undercuts the pure "small-model-only" narrative and adds a dependency that may affect reproducibility/cost in practice.

Precision/recall analysis (Table 3, Table 4, Appendix F) shows ToolV has relatively low recall and can filter out correct solutions due to imperfect code generation (false negatives), a limitation the paper acknowledges but does not resolve, and which appears in the Geometry category and Level 5 problems where ToolV actually hurts performance.

Applicability is inherently restricted to domains where correctness is tool-verifiable (arithmetic/code execution, fact retrieval); results on the more open-ended MMLU-Pro knowledge tasks are noticeably weaker and less consistent than on math benchmarks, and the retriever-based fact-checking pipeline is fairly simplistic (BM25 over Wikipedia abstracts, no reranking/query rewriting).

Some comparisons could be strengthened — e.g., a more direct compute-matched comparison against simply scaling verifier size versus ToolV beyond the single Figure 7 case, and broader baselines beyond Themis for the tool-integration comparison.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: whether small LMs can reliably verify solutions under test-time scaling is underexplored, and the concept-proof experiment (Fig. 1b) nicely illustrates the memorization gap that motivates the approach.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three small model families (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B), two verifier types (PRM and GenRM), and two/three datasets (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro subset in appendix).

Includes useful ablations: compute-budget-normalized comparisons (Fig. 10/11), data efficiency of distillation (Fig. 15), category/difficulty breakdown (Fig. 6), and a comparison against a prior tool-augmented reward modeling baseline (Themis).

Provides a formal (if simplified) theoretical treatment connecting tool use to reduced memorization requirements and to monotonic improvement of best-of-N under a less noisy verifier, which at least gives conceptual grounding for the empirical claims.

Reasonably transparent reproducibility/ethics statements, with prompts and hyperparameters detailed in the appendix, and honest discussion of failure cases (false negatives from faulty generated code).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core mechanism (offloading calculation/fact-checking to a code interpreter or retriever) closely follows established tool-integrated reasoning work (PAL, ToRA, CRITIC, Toolformer, Themis); the paper's contribution is largely a two-stage filter-then-score pipeline applied specifically to the verification step, which is an incremental combination rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The theoretical analysis is highly stylized (a toy a+b=c memorization task, a binary coin-flip generator/verifier model) and only loosely connects to the actual complexity of math/knowledge verification tasks used in experiments; it functions more as a post-hoc intuition-builder than a rigorous justification of the proposed method's real-world behavior.

Some headline comparisons may be unfair or inflated: comparing a 1B model with ToolV against an 8B model without tool access (Fig. 3) conflates the benefit of tool use with model scale rather than isolating the verification-capacity argument cleanly; a tool-equipped 8B baseline is not shown in the main comparison.

The knowledge-intensive extension (MMLU-Pro) is relegated to the appendix and shows noisier, weaker gains with retrieved documents; the paper leans on an oracle 'gold documents' setting (generated by GPT-4o) to demonstrate large improvements, which is an unrealistic upper bound and somewhat overstates the practical potential of the method outside math.

Baselines are somewhat weak/limited: 'zero-shot GenRM' without any fine-tuning is close to a strawman comparison, and comparison to prior tool-integrated verifiers (Themis) is confined to a single setting/figure rather than a systematic evaluation.

The compute-overhead justification (a 1.14x scaling factor derived from average token counts) is a rough heuristic that ignores wall-clock latency of code execution/retrieval calls and does not robustly establish that ToolV is compute-optimal versus simply scaling the verifier or generator.

Acknowledged but under-quantified limitation: ToolV acts only as a rejection filter and can produce false negatives due to incorrect generated code (Table 4 shows notably low recall, ~0.69-0.73), which could meaningfully cap real-world gains; the paper does not explore mitigations despite noting this as future work.

Reliance on a single teacher model (gpt-4o-mini) for distillation without analysis of how teacher quality bounds student performance, raising questions about robustness/generalizability of the distillation-based pipeline.

Evaluation is essentially confined to math reasoning (plus a small knowledge-intensive appendix experiment); no evidence is given for other domains where tool integration for verification might be less straightforward (e.g., code correctness, commonsense reasoning), limiting the generality of the claimed contribution.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether small language models can perform reliable verification for test-time scaling without relying on large verifier models, with a compelling concept-proof experiment (Fig. 1) that clearly demonstrates the memorization bottleneck sLMs face in arithmetic verification and how tool use alleviates it.

The proposed two-stage Tool-integrated Verification (T1/ToolV) framework is simple, generalizable, and shown to integrate seamlessly with both PRM and GenRM-style verifiers, which is a practically useful design choice.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three small model families (SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B) and two benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K), plus an extension to knowledge-intensive multi-domain tasks (MMLU-Pro) in the appendix.
Strong headline result: a 1B model combined with ToolV can outperform an 8B model, which is a meaningful and practically significant demonstration of the method's value for efficient deployment.

Thorough set of supporting analyses, including comparisons with a relevant prior baseline (Themis), ablations isolating the necessity of the two-stage design, data efficiency of distillation, and careful discussion/normalization of computational overhead (token cost accounting) to ensure gains aren't merely due to extra compute.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed appendix with hyperparameters, prompts, dataset splits, and stated intent to release code/prompts.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Section 5) relies on highly simplified, toy settings (memorizing single-digit addition tables, binary generator/verifier noise models) that only loosely map onto the actual empirical setup (code-based verification of multi-step math solutions, LLM-based PRM/GenRM). The theorems are illustrative rather than providing guarantees relevant to the real system, and this gap between theory and practice is not fully acknowledged beyond a brief disclaimer.

ToolV acts purely as a rejection filter and cannot correct false negatives (correct solutions wrongly filtered out); this is an important limitation that could meaningfully cap performance, and it is only briefly mentioned in the conclusion without deeper empirical analysis of its practical severity across benchmarks.

The method's technical novelty is somewhat incremental — it combines existing ideas (program-aided verification, LLM distillation, generative reward models) into a two-stage pipeline rather than proposing fundamentally new techniques.

Performance gains are inconsistent across problem types and difficulty levels (e.g., drops at MATH Level 5 and in Geometry, per Fig. 6), and the MMLU-Pro results are noisy and heavily dependent on retrieval quality (large gap between retrieved vs. gold documents), suggesting limited robustness of the approach outside well-suited calculation-heavy domains.

The approach is restricted to parallel best-of-N scaling; extensions to sequential or search-based test-time scaling (which the paper cites as increasingly popular, e.g., DeepSeek-R1/s1) are left entirely to future work, limiting the generality of the claimed contribution.

The case study (Appendix F) shows that ToolV's own code generation can introduce new errors (e.g., symbolic equality mismatches), and the reported precision/recall trade-offs (Table 4) indicate non-trivial false-negative rates, which somewhat undercuts the reliability narrative central to the paper's motivation.
Reliance on a moderately capable proprietary teacher model (gpt-4o-mini) for distillation adds a dependency and cost that is not deeply analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to teacher quality).
